name: Fasting for face fat

lead: Fasting for face fat means using intermittent fasting, such as a daily eating window, alternate days or 5:2, to lose body fat and reveal a leaner, more defined face. It sits alongside cutting and 'leanmaxxing' and hollow-cheek aesthetics.

Fasting lowers calorie intake and lengthens overnight fasting intervals. A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials in 6,582 adults found weight loss roughly comparable to ordinary calorie restriction. No study has measured facial fat after fasting, and where fat comes off varies by person and genetics.

paras: Most people pick a time-restricted window or a few lower-calorie days a week and pair it with their usual cutting routine. Weight changes show up over weeks to months, and faces slim as overall body fat falls. Some report that people with low body fat still keep fuller faces.

Hunger, irritability, dizziness and headache are reported. Fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, underweight people or those prone to eating disorders. Forum members raise concerns about testosterone, thyroid and muscle, and a 2025 Cell study reported that intermittent fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration.

chain: Calorie intake and body fat fall
angle.text: Users adopt intermittent fasting to lower overall calorie intake and body fat, which slims the face and sharpens cheek and jaw definition. Trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie reduction; how much of it comes off the face varies by person.

lead: Fasting for face fat is the use of intermittent fasting patterns, such as daily time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting or 5:2 schedules, with the aim of lowering body fat and thereby slimming the face.[1][2] The appearance logic is a chain: a fasting schedule makes it easier for some people to eat fewer calories, lower body fat follows, and a leaner body can bring out jaw, cheekbone and under-eye definition that a fuller face hides.[3][4] The practice sits within looksmaxxing discussions of cutting, 'leanmaxxing' and hollow-cheek aesthetics.[3]

Intermittent fasting as a diet has a documented history running from early 20th-century obesity studies through the 2012 BBC Horizon documentary that popularised the 5:2 pattern and the 2018 survey that named it the most popular diet of the year.[1] A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials in 6,582 adults compared intermittent fasting with continuous energy restriction and unrestricted eating for body weight and cardiometabolic outcomes and described fasting as a viable weight-loss approach with results generally comparable to continuous restriction.[5] The American Heart Association and the US National Institute on Aging have described evidence for wider benefits as limited.[1][6]

Faces lose fat unevenly and on an individual schedule. The buccal fat pad, a deep pad of fat in the cheek, is associated in anatomical writing with hollow cheeks, and no published study has measured how any diet changes it or other facial fat compartments.[7] Members of looksmax.org and lifting forums trade reports on both sides: some say continued leaning improved their faces, others describe people who stay lean in the body and keep a fuller face.
infobox: About 2.5% to 9.9% of body weight (per Wikipedia)[1]

paras: Intermittent fasting covers several schedules. Time-restricted eating confines food to a daily window, often 8 to 12 hours, and can be timed to daylight. One-meal-a-day (OMAD) compresses all food into a one-to-two-hour window. Alternate-day fasting alternates fast days, with either no calories or up to a quarter of usual needs, with ordinary eating days. The 5:2 diet limits two non-consecutive days a week to roughly 500 to 600 calories. Periodic fasts are water-only fasts longer than 24 hours.[1]

Reviewers describe a progression through metabolic states during a fast, from a fed state of about four hours, to a post-absorptive state, to a fasted state after 12 to 36 hours in which fat is mobilised and ketones are produced, sometimes called the metabolic switch.[1][8] The attraction for appearance-minded dieters is mostly practical: a short eating window or a fast day gives a clear rule that some people find easier to follow than counting calories every day.[3][4]

Fasting is ancient and appears in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism and Judaism.[1] Therapeutic fasting for obesity was studied as early as 1915, and medical interest revived in the 1960s after Bloom and colleagues published an enthusiastic report; early fasts ranged from one to 14 days, and clinicians warned against unmonitored use when lay magazines picked up the idea.[1]

The 5:2 pattern was first documented in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie, Mark Mattson and colleagues, and British broadcaster Michael Mosley popularised it in 2012 with the BBC Horizon documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer, followed by the 2013 book The Fast Diet written with Mimi Spencer.[1][9] Mosley continued to write on fasting and low-carbohydrate eating in later books before his death in June 2024.[9]

A 2019 New England Journal of Medicine review of intermittent fasting, health, aging and disease brought the topic into mainstream medical literature, and a 2018 Obesity paper on the metabolic switch and a 2003 PNAS paper from the Mattson group are among the most-cited papers in the area.[10][8][11] Wikipedia reports that intermittent fasting was the most popular diet in 2018 in an International Food Information Council survey, with companies selling coaching, supplements and meal packages around it, a market critics described as expensive and weakly evidenced.[1]

On looksmax.org, threads on intermittent fasting go back to the forum's earliest years and ask whether fasting is a good tool for losing body fat, how to run an eating window, and how fasting compares with other approaches.[3][4][12][13] The surrounding vocabulary includes cutting, leanmaxxing and the idea of an optimal body-fat range for facial definition.[3][14]

Several members describe pairing fasting with training to preserve muscle, and some ask whether fasting costs muscle or interacts with growth-hormone use.[15][16] Lifting forums such as T Nation host parallel discussions, including a member asking whether muscle can be built while fasting 16 to 20 hours on non-training days.[17]

Not all reports are favourable. A T Nation poster wrote that intermittent fasting had been a disaster for them and that their body and face were finally 'unswelling' after they stopped; another said it was great for studying but poor for building muscle and contributed to binge eating; a third attributed a drop in libido to fasting combined with chronic undereating.[18][19][20]

Proponents describe fasting as a simple route to a calorie deficit and cite research on autophagy and hair follicles; one looksmax.org thread summarising a video argues that autophagy supports hair growth and that fasting, exercise and metformin induce it, citing Cell Reports, PLoS Biology and NEJM papers.[12] Others in the community point the other way, listing possible falls in IGF-1, testosterone and thyroid hormones and rises in hunger-related stress hormones as costs.[21]
Some members hold that very low body fat is needed for a defined face, while others call low body fat alone insufficient if the face stays full for genetic reasons.

Weight loss. The 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis searched Medline, Embase and Central to November 2024, pooled 99 randomized trials with 6,582 adults (720 healthy, 5,862 with existing health conditions) and graded the certainty of evidence with GRADE.[5] Wikipedia summarises most human studies as showing weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent, with the loss coming mainly from fat plus some lean mass; for time-restricted eating a fat-to-lean ratio of 4:1 is reported.[1]

Metabolic outcomes. Reviews describe improvements in some cardiometabolic markers and propose roles for circadian biology, the gut microbiome and sleep.[2][8][22] An early controlled trial of early time-restricted feeding in men with prediabetes reported better insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress even without weight loss.[23]

Athletes. A trial in resistance-trained men tested eight weeks of 16/8 time-restricted feeding on metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation and cardiovascular risk factors.[24] Wikipedia states that intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance and that overnight fasting reduces performance in exercise longer than about 60 minutes.[1]

Guidelines. The US National Institute on Aging describes the research as limited and inconclusive and does not recommend intermittent fasting for the general public; the American Heart Association statement on meal timing reviewed intermittent fasting alongside breakfast skipping and meal frequency and described the evidence for cardiovascular benefit as limited.[1][6] The NHS advises people considering 5:2 to consult a physician first.[1]

Hair. A 2025 Cell paper reported that intermittent fasting suppressed hair follicle regeneration through inter-organ signalling, which is relevant to forum concerns about hair.[25] Laboratory work on autophagy in hair follicles is cited by proponents, and no trial shows that fasting prevents balding.[12][25]

No published study measures facial fat change from fasting. The buccal fat pad lies between the buccinator and masseter and zygomaticus muscles, is linked with hollow cheeks, loses volume between childhood and adulthood, and is distinct from the malar and jowl fat compartments; surgical removal to reduce cheek fullness carries a risk of damage to the buccal branch of the facial nerve and the parotid ducts.[7]
Forum threads describe people with low body fat who retain a fuller face and ask whether genetics explains it, while others report that continued leaning improved their face.

sections.h: Reported risks and who is advised to avoid it
paras: Short-term side effects reported include persistent hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, which Wikipedia says fade within about a month for many people; dropout in trials ranged from 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting and 0 to 50 percent for continuous restriction in a 2019 review.[1]

Health bodies cited by Wikipedia advise against intermittent fasting for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, people with or vulnerable to eating disorders, people with insulin-dependent diabetes and underweight people.[1] A 2022 review concluded intermittent fasting could be considered for people with unhealthy weight gain but said longer-term outcomes need more research and that it should be avoided in some health conditions.[2]

Among lifters, a forum poster characterised fasting plus restrictive diets as a quick pathway to an eating disorder, and others describe binge eating after fasting.[19][26] Adverse effects have not been comprehensively studied, according to Wikipedia.[1]

No studies found of fasting for facial fat specifically. Human trials of intermittent fasting examine body weight, glucose control, blood pressure and lipids, including a 2025 network meta-analysis of 99 randomized trials, a 5:2 meal-replacement trial in adults with early type 2 diabetes, and a randomized trial of 16:8 and 14:10 schedules in people with obesity and type 2 diabetes.[5][27][28]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, intermittent fasting is discussed as a weight-loss tool, a possible hair-health aid via autophagy, and a possible hormonal risk; lifting forums add reports of muscle loss and binge eating.[12][21][19]
